title: Registration, DNS, and routing
summary: Bindings, DNS location, loose routing, outbound flows, Path, Service-Route, GRUU, and forking.

lessons.title: REGISTER and bindings
lessons.summary: REGISTER binds an address-of-record to one or more Contacts, and the registrar is a different role from the proxy.
objectives: Point To at the address-of-record and Contact at the binding
Refresh with the same Call-ID and a higher CSeq
Handle 423 by raising the expiry to Min-Expires

illustration.title: Binding operations
illustration.caption: The 200 OK lists the bindings the registrar is holding after the request.
rows: Expires header or the expires parameter
No other Contact on that request

sections.h: The registrar writes, the proxy reads
paragraphs: Section 10 makes REGISTER the way a UA publishes a Contact for an address-of-record. The To URI is that address-of-record. The Contact URI is the binding. A proxy later consults the location service when an INVITE arrives for the address-of-record.

The registrar and the proxy are different roles. One product often runs both, and the trace still shows REGISTER going to the registrar function and INVITE going to the proxy function. REGISTER does not create a dialog you can BYE. You refresh it with another REGISTER.

Use one Call-ID for the binding and increase CSeq on each REGISTER. The 200 OK returns the current bindings. A 401 carries WWW-Authenticate, and the retry carries Authorization. That challenge is section 22, the same digest model as other UAS challenges, not a 407.

If the requested expiry is shorter than the registrar allows, the response is 423 Interval Too Brief and it includes Min-Expires. Retry with an expiry at least that large. A q parameter on Contact is a preference from 0 to 1, and a larger q is preferred when a proxy forks.

steps.label: REGISTER
steps.note: To is the address-of-record. Contact is the binding. Expires is 3600.
steps.message:
REGISTER sip:example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKreg1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:alice@example.com>
Call-ID: reg-1@example.com
CSeq: 1 REGISTER
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>;expires=3600
Expires: 3600
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: WWW-Authenticate is a registrar challenge. This is not a dialog.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 401 Unauthorized

From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=regtag
Call-ID: reg-1@example.com
CSeq: 1 REGISTER
WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="example.com", nonce="abc123", algorithm=MD5
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Same Call-ID, CSeq 2, Authorization present. The binding is requested again.
steps.message:
REGISTER sip:example.com SIP/2.0

Max-Forwards: 70

Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKreg2

quiz.why: Products combine them. The specification separates them.

check.why: Min-Expires on this response is 3600. 90 is the session-timer floor, not this header.

fault.title: BYE sent to unregister
fault.symptom: A phone sends BYE to the registrar to clear a binding. The registrar answers 481 and the Contact remains.
fault.log:
BYE sip:example.com SIP/2.0
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:alice@example.com>
Call-ID: reg-1@example.com
CSeq: 3 BYE

SIP/2.0 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist
choices: REGISTER with expires 0 removes a binding. BYE is not registration.
The To URI must be a GRUU
fault.why: Registration is not a dialog. There is nothing for BYE to terminate.
fault.cause: The client used the dialog teardown method on the registrar.
fault.fix: Send REGISTER with the same Call-ID, the next CSeq, and Contact expires=0. Use Contact: * and Expires: 0 only when every binding should go.

lessons.title: Locating a server with RFC 3263
lessons.summary: RFC 3263 turns a SIP domain into a transport, a port, and an address with NAPTR, SRV, and A or AAAA.
objectives: Order NAPTR, then SRV, then A or AAAA
Name the SIP+D2U, SIP+D2T, and SIPS+D2T services
Skip the name lookup when the Request-URI is already an IP address

illustration.title: Lookup order
illustration.caption: An explicit transport or port skips the records that are no longer needed. A numeric IP skips the name.

sections.h: The domain is not the socket
paragraphs: When the Request-URI host is a domain and the URI does not already dictate transport and port, RFC 3263 starts with NAPTR. The services you will see are SIP+D2U for UDP, SIP+D2T for TCP, and SIPS+D2T for TLS. The NAPTR result names the SRV name to query.

SRV returns a host name and a port. A or AAAA turns that host into an address. The client then writes Via with the transport it selected and sends the SIP request. The DNS messages are not SIP messages. They happen before the first arrow on this ladder.

A numeric IP address in the Request-URI does not need NAPTR or SRV. An explicit port skips the SRV lookup and goes to A or AAAA. An explicit transport parameter selects the NAPTR service instead of leaving the choice open.

Hard-coding 198.51.100.30 will place the next request on that address and will not notice when the SRV target moves. Keep the domain in the Request-URI when you want RFC 3263 to run, and keep the documentation ranges of RFC 5737 out of production.

SIP+D2T is TCP. SIPS+D2T is TLS.
A or AAAA then resolves the host.

choices: Requires a NAPTR query for the IP
quiz.why: There is no domain to look up.
SIPS selects a protected transport. D2T is the TCP service.

quiz.q: Responses find the previous hop by
quiz.why: DNS chooses where a request goes. Via chooses where a response goes.

cards.back: Selects the SIP service, such as SIP+D2U or SIP+D2T.
Host and port for the selected service.
Addresses for the SRV target.
No domain lookup. Send to that address.

lab.title: What happened before the INVITE
lab.prompt: The first note states the DNS result. The SIP itself contains no NAPTR records.
steps: Name the record that would have supplied a port.

check.why: NAPTR picks the service. SRV picks host and port. The m= line is media.

fault.title: IP pinned, SRV moved
fault.symptom: The peer moved in DNS. The SBC still sends to 192.0.2.40 because the dial-peer target is a literal address. Calls time out.
fault.log:
dial-peer voice 10 voip

DNS SRV for example.com now points at a different host
INVITE retransmits, no response
choices: The literal target never consults the new SRV
SRV is consulted on every IP target
5060 means use NAPTR even with an IP
fault.why: RFC 3263 runs on a domain. An address skips it.
fault.cause: The session target was pinned to an address that is no longer the SRV result.
fault.fix: Target the domain and let NAPTR and SRV run, or update the address when operations change DNS.

lessons.title: Loose routing and Max-Forwards
lessons.summary: With lr, the Request-URI stays the remote target, each hop pops its own Route, and Max-Forwards of 0 yields 483.
objectives: Pop a top Route that names this hop
Leave the Request-URI in place when lr is present
Return 483 when Max-Forwards arrives as 0

illustration.title: Two counters on a forwarded request
illustration.caption: Route is the path. Max-Forwards is the budget. They are not substitutes.

paragraphs: A loose router looks at the top Route. If that URI names this hop, the hop removes it. The Request-URI stays the remote target because the Route URI contains lr. The hop then forwards to the next Route, or to the Request-URI when the route set is empty.

Strict routing is the older behavior for a Route URI without lr. Section 16.4 will rewrite the Request-URI in that case. Proxies that follow RFC 3261 put lr on Record-Route so the target the UAC wrote is still the target at the end of the path.

The UAC sets Max-Forwards, and the value SHOULD be 70. A proxy that forwards decrements it by one. If a request arrives with Max-Forwards 0, the proxy does not forward it. For an INVITE that means 483 Too Many Hops.

OPTIONS is the exception that may be answered locally when Max-Forwards is already 0. A loop that should have been a 482 Loop Detected is a different check, based on Via. Do not use 483 as the name for every loop.

steps.label: BYE
steps.note: Request-URI is the peer. First Route is Edge, and it has lr. Max-Forwards is 70.

BYE sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKlse1

Route: <sip:203.0.113.20;lr>
Route: <sip:198.51.100.30;lr>

To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 3 BYE
Content-Length: 0

Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com

Is replaced by the top Route

quiz.why: Each forward decrements it by one.

quiz.why: OPTIONS may be answered locally. An INVITE is not forwarded.
483 is the hop budget. 482 is the loop check.

quiz.why: Edge pops that value. Core is the remaining Route.

lab.title: Watch Route shrink
lab.prompt: Compare the Route headers on the first and second BYE.
steps: Confirm the Request-URI host did not become the proxy.

check.q: After Edge forwards the BYE, the remaining Route is
check.why: Edge removed the Route that named itself. Core is still on the path.

fault.title: Forwarded with Max-Forwards 0
fault.symptom: A proxy receives an INVITE with Max-Forwards 0 and sends it on. The next proxy also forwards it. The loop never returns 483.
fault.log:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.20;branch=z9hG4bKloop1
Max-Forwards: 0

Proxy log: forwarding INVITE, Max-Forwards still 0
choices: The proxy must return 483 and not forward
The proxy should reset the value to 70
fault.why: Zero means the budget is spent. Decrement happens only when the value is greater than zero and the proxy is actually forwarding.
fault.fix: If Max-Forwards is 0, send 483 Too Many Hops for this INVITE. Do not put it back to 70.

lessons.title: Outbound, reg-id, and keepalives
lessons.summary: RFC 5626 binds a UA instance to one or more flows with reg-id and +sip.instance, and keepalives hold those flows open.
objectives: Read reg-id and +sip.instance on Contact
Tell a second flow from a refresh of the first
Name the keepalive used on TCP and on UDP

illustration.title: Same instance, two flows
illustration.caption: The instance URN stays. reg-id changes when the flow changes.
rows: CRLF on TCP, STUN on UDP

paragraphs: RFC 5626 identifies the UA instance with the Contact parameter +sip.instance, whose value is a URN, commonly a UUID URN. reg-id is a positive integer that names one registration flow for that instance.

A second REGISTER with the same instance and a different reg-id is a second flow, which is how a UA keeps a backup path. The same instance and the same reg-id is a refresh of that flow. Supported: outbound is how the UA asks for this behavior. The edge proxy and the registrar use the flow the REGISTER arrived on when they send a later request back.

On TCP and TLS the keepalive is a double CRLF. The peer answers with a single CRLF. On UDP the keepalive is STUN. These messages are defined so a NAT binding and the connection stay up, and so a dead flow can be detected.

A keepalive has no Request-URI, no CSeq, and no dialog. If a trace shows only CRLF on the SIP port, that can be the outbound keepalive rather than a broken INVITE. The SIP registration beside it is what created the flow.

steps.label: REGISTER
steps.note: reg-id 1 and the instance URN. Supported includes outbound.
steps.message:
REGISTER sip:example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKout1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:alice@example.com>
Call-ID: reg-flow1@example.com
CSeq: 1 REGISTER
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>;reg-id=1;+sip.instance="<urn:uuid:00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001>"
Supported: outbound, path
Expires: 3600
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Require: outbound means this registrar is doing the extension.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKout1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=out1

Require: outbound

Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Same instance, reg-id 2. This is a second flow, not a refresh.
steps.message:
REGISTER sip:example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKout2

choices: One registration flow of a UA instance
quiz.why: The instance URN identifies the UA. reg-id splits its flows.

choices: A URN naming the UA instance
quiz.why: It stays constant across reg-id values for that UA.

quiz.q: Same instance and a new reg-id means
quiz.why: Same reg-id would refresh the existing flow.

quiz.q: The TCP keepalive in RFC 5626 is
choices: A double CRLF, answered by a single CRLF
quiz.why: UDP uses STUN. Neither keepalive is a SIP request.
Registration itself remains RFC 3261 section 10. The flow parameters are 5626.

quiz.q: A later request to the UA is sent
choices: On the flow that REGISTER used
To the AOR host with a fresh NAPTR only
quiz.why: That is why the flow has to stay open.

cards.back: Identifies one flow. A new value is a new flow.
URN for the UA instance, stable across flows.
Double CRLF on connection-oriented transports. Single CRLF answers.
The UDP keepalive in the outbound specification.

lab.title: Count the flows
lab.prompt: Dissect the second 200 OK. Two Contact headers share an instance and differ by reg-id.
lab.message:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKout2
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=out2
Call-ID: reg-flow2@example.com
CSeq: 1 REGISTER
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>;reg-id=1;+sip.instance="<urn:uuid:00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001>";expires=3590
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>;reg-id=2;+sip.instance="<urn:uuid:00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001>";expires=3600
Content-Length: 0

check.q: How many outbound flows does this 200 advertise?
check.why: reg-id 1 and reg-id 2 are both present for the same instance.

fault.title: Second flow treated as a replacement
fault.symptom: The UA registers reg-id 2 for redundancy. The registrar drops reg-id 1. An outage on the second path leaves the UA unreachable.
fault.log:
REGISTER Contact reg-id=2;+sip.instance="<urn:uuid:00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001>"
200 OK Contact: only reg-id=2
(reg-id 1 missing)
choices: Same instance and a different reg-id must keep both bindings
fault.why: A refresh reuses reg-id. A new reg-id is an additional flow.
fault.cause: The registrar keyed only on the address-of-record and the instance, and ignored reg-id.
fault.fix: Store the binding by instance plus reg-id. Return both Contacts in the 200 OK.

lessons.title: Path and Service-Route
lessons.summary: Path is the inbound vector stored with a binding, and Service-Route is the outbound vector the registrar gives the UA.
objectives: Insert Path on REGISTER the way a proxy inserts Record-Route
Use Service-Route as a preloaded Route for a new request
Keep the two vectors from being swapped

illustration.title: In versus out
illustration.caption: Both headers look like Route URIs. They are learned at registration and they point in opposite directions.

layers.name: Path
layers.detail: Edge inserts it. Registrar stores it with the binding.

layers.name: Inbound INVITE
layers.detail: Registrar puts that Path on the Route toward the UA.

layers.name: Service-Route
layers.detail: Registrar returns it in the 200 OK.

sections.h: Path is Record-Route for a binding
paragraphs: RFC 3327 defines Path. A proxy between the UA and the registrar inserts a Path URI, with lr, on the REGISTER. The registrar stores that vector with the Contact. The 200 OK echoes Path so the UA can see it.

When a request later arrives for that address-of-record, the registrar or home proxy places the stored Path into Route so the request reaches the UA through the same edge. Path is not the dialog route set. The dialog route set still comes from Record-Route on the INVITE.

RFC 3608 defines Service-Route. The registrar puts it on the 200 OK to REGISTER. The UA saves those URIs and uses them as a preloaded Route on requests that are not yet inside a dialog, such as the first INVITE.

Service-Route does not tell the network how to reach the UA. Path does that. Swapping them sends the outbound call back at the UA or sends the inbound call at the home proxy with no edge. Supported: path is how the UA indicates it understands the inbound vector.

lessons.title: GRUU and a single instance
lessons.summary: A GRUU routes to one UA instance, and the registrar returns it as pub-gruu or temp-gruu on the binding.
objectives: Register with Supported: gruu and +sip.instance
Distinguish a public GRUU from a temporary GRUU
Expect an AOR to fork and a GRUU to target one instance

illustration.title: Where the request can land
illustration.caption: The gr parameter marks a GRUU. The instance URN is what the registrar bound.
rows: Hides the AOR and can change

sections.h: Ask for a URI that means this instance
paragraphs: RFC 5627 defines the GRUU. The UA registers with Supported: gruu and a +sip.instance URN on the Contact. The registrar returns pub-gruu and temp-gruu parameters on that Contact in the 200 OK.

A public GRUU is stable enough to hand to another party. It is often the address-of-record plus a gr parameter that carries the instance. A temporary GRUU is minted so the far end cannot use it to learn the address-of-record, and the registrar can change it.

An INVITE to the address-of-record may fork to every Contact. An INVITE to a GRUU is routed to the instance that registered that GRUU. The gr parameter is the marker that this URI is a GRUU rather than an ordinary address-of-record.

The home proxy still uses Path or the registered flow to reach the instance. A GRUU does not mean the Contact IP is globally reachable. It means the logical target is one UA, not the whole set of bindings.

lessons.title: Forking and early dialogs
lessons.summary: A forking proxy creates one client transaction per binding, and each To tag is a separate early dialog.
objectives: Give each branch its own Via branch
Key early dialogs on the remote tag
Forward every 2xx and cancel other branches on a 6xx

illustration.title: One INVITE, two early dialogs
illustration.caption: Call-ID and the From tag match. The To tags do not. That is two dialogs.

sections.h: One server transaction, many client transactions
paragraphs: A stateful proxy that forks sends a separate client transaction to each target. Each gets its own Via branch. The Call-ID, From tag, and CSeq number stay the ones from the caller. 100 Trying from a downstream branch is not forwarded. The proxy already generated 100 on the upstream hop if it needed to.

A provisional response with a To tag creates an early dialog for that branch. Two 180 responses with different To tags are two early dialogs, even though the Call-ID matches. The UAC has to keep both.

sections.h: What a final response does to the other branches
paragraphs: A 2xx is forwarded immediately, and another 2xx on a different branch is also forwarded. The UAC ACKs each 2xx. The application can BYE the dialog it will not keep. A proxy does not treat the first 200 OK as permission to invent a CANCEL for the others.

A 6xx is different. The proxy should cancel the client transactions that are still pending and it must not open new branches. It does not forward the 6xx until that cancel step has run, so the caller does not see a 6xx followed by a 2xx. Other 4xx and 5xx responses wait so the proxy can choose the best one after the branches settle.

choices: Forwards it and can also forward a later 200 from another branch

fault.title: First 200 cancelled the other branch
fault.symptom: Phone A answers. The proxy sends CANCEL to Phone B and then Phone B's 200 OK arrives anyway. The caller never sees it.
fault.log:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
To tag=tagA
Proxy log: CANCEL branch z9hG4bKforkB because a 200 arrived
SIP/2.0 200 OK
To tag=tagB
Proxy log: dropped, branch already cancelled
choices: A 2xx must still be forwarded. CANCEL is not how a proxy suppresses a second 200
The second 200 is illegal once the first exists
To tags must be equal when forking
The proxy should ACK tagB itself and discard it
fault.why: The specification forwards every 2xx. The UAC decides which dialog to keep.
fault.cause: The proxy applied the 6xx cancel rule to a 200 OK.
fault.fix: Forward both 200 OK responses. Let the UAC ACK them and send BYE on the dialog it will not use.
